Open Grant Proposals

  • Zcash Private Receive Bridge

  • Applicant requests $38,000 over about 10 months to harden and release “Private Receive Bridge,” a local Rust service that sits between an unmodified desktop Zcash wallet and a remote lightwalletd server. Instead of letting the wallet ask the server for specific transactions, which reveals which ones it cares about, the bridge downloads every full transaction in a block range and serves the wallet from a local cache. Funding covers wallet qualification, daemon hardening, a Linux release, an $8,000 independent review and 6 months of maintenance.

  • Artkor: I hope that once Tachyon is implemented this problem will become much less significant, but for now I’m not convinced the proposed architecture offers a meaningful privacy improvement for end users. Quite the opposite: I’m concerned it could introduce additional privacy risks. I believe using Tor or Nym, built into wallets or as an external privacy layer, is a much simpler and more practical approach. I don’t see a compelling reason to fund another layer of infrastructure at this point. I decline.

  • Hanh: I decline as well. The solution is too heavy for regular users because it requires installing a server and uses about as much disk space as running Zebra plus an indexer. In the future, the better solution will be a PIR (private information retrieval) server. There are plans to deploy servers that let you retrieve any transaction privately. With that protocol you would download compact blocks as usual and then fetch transactions anonymously, without installing anything locally.

  • Paul: I would also like to decline, for similar reasons. I’ve heard about other solutions coming online very soon, in particular OHTTP, that will help with this. But I very much appreciate the work and the proposal.

  • Gguy: I agree. I’ve heard of some teams beginning to work on PIR, so I’d like to see how those solutions pan out. It’s a decline.

  • Zerodartz: Decline, I agree with others.

  • Declined

  • Konclave: taking the viewing key off the coordinator

  • Applicant requests $18,000 over about 19 weeks to remove full viewing keys from the hosted coordinator of Konclave, its FROST-based group vault for Zcash. Today the coordinator stores every vault’s viewing key unencrypted. The work moves key custody, scanning and proving onto members’ own devices: benchmark and design first (with an independent review), then new vaults where the viewing key never leaves a member’s device, then migration of existing vaults. Applicant will also publish a reusable pattern for other Zcash teams.

  • Artkor: I’m glad to see this proposal because it comes from a real need for FROST within a local Zcash community, and that’s exactly the kind of practical use case I like to see. I think this is a reasonable experiment to support, especially with the independent technical review and milestone-based funding. The first milestone should establish whether the proposed approach is practical before moving forward. I approve.

  • Hanh: I would approve as well because I’d like to encourage people to try these things, but I honestly don’t think this proposal is going the right way. The first milestone, measuring performance, covers something other wallets have already done, since it’s essentially putting a wallet in the browser, and the other pieces have also largely been done by other projects. I’m not super convinced about this project, but I’d like to see them try it out and see where it goes.

  • Paul: I would approve as well. I have similar feelings of uncertainty here, but it’s a modest request with milestones that seem reasonable, so I’d like to see how this turns out.

  • Gguy: I will also approve. I think that encouraging exploration in this area is a good thing, and given the reasonable cost of this one, I’m ready to approve.

  • Zerodartz: I’m personally skeptical. There might be some demand for this, but I’m not 100% sure if there’s enough right now, so I’m going to decline.

  • Approved (Zerodartz declined)

  • ZEC Order Pay: shielded ZEC checkout, refunds and creator payouts for service marketplaces

  • Applicant requests $36,000 over about 5 months to build ZEC Order Pay, an MIT-licensed Python library with a small Rust helper that lets web marketplaces take shielded ZEC per order. Each order gets its own Unified Address and ZIP-321 QR code. Payments are detected with a viewing key only, so no spending keys sit on the server. The library also handles underpayment, expiry and refunds, and prepares batched creator payouts as unsigned transactions to be signed offline. It would be demonstrated live on Applicant’s own marketplace, titanhold.app.

  • Artkor: I think the applicant could benefit from exploring the existing Zcash payment solutions that other services already use to accept ZEC. For now, I don’t see a compelling need to fund a separate implementation. I decline.

  • Paul: I decline as well. Even the applicant noted that there’s overlap and that they want to avoid it. Maybe they could research that first, figure out where there isn’t overlap, and submit another grant for that area.

  • Gguy: I’m also not convinced. I decline.

  • Zerodartz: I think our current payment solutions are good enough and cover most use cases, so I don’t see much extra benefit from this one. I’m declining.

  • Hanh: I decline as well. The applicant didn’t give a strong reason for not using the existing solutions, and from reading the grant it feels like they want to reinvent the wheel.

  • Gguy: Yes, reinventing the wheel feels like something we’ve seen from some AI models.

  • Declined

  • Interoperable FROST co-signing for shielded ZEC: open specs and a reference implementation

  • Applicant requests $16,500 over 11 weeks for an open spec covering 2-of-3 FROST multisig for shielded ZEC across the user’s own devices. The spec defines encrypted QR messages between the coordinating device and co-signers (no server), plus a share backup format with an option that needs no recovery phrase. Applicant would also deliver a standalone Rust crate on crates.io, test vectors, a tamper test suite, and a reference implementation in OpenPGP Wallet, Applicant’s Rust/Tauri desktop wallet, with spends shown on testnet and mainnet. The goal is to stop NoirWallet, Zkool and others from each shipping FROST co-signing that can’t work with the others.

  • Artkor: After our last discussion, I’m leaning toward the idea that an effort to standardize FROST at this early stage would be very valuable. It’s much easier to establish common standards now than to deal with incompatible implementations later. However, I’m still not fully confident in the applicant’s track record, so I remain neutral on this proposal. That said, the milestone-based payment structure limits our risk if the work isn’t delivered, so if others support it, I’d be willing to support it too.

  • Gguy: I think I’m going to approve this one today. While this may not get us to the final solution and FROST interoperability, I think more people entering this discussion is a good thing. I approve.

  • Hanh: I have a couple of concerns about this proposal. A minor one is that it overlaps with what I’ve done in Zkool, though that’s not too bad, since if it becomes a standard I’d have less work to do. The bigger one is that there’s no ZIP as a deliverable. Without one, I’m afraid it wouldn’t be a standard that, for example, the ZODL team would acknowledge, and it may not work out because of that. Writing a ZIP is significantly harder than implementing the standard. If they add a requirement to write a ZIP, I would support it. Without a ZIP, I won’t.

  • Paul: I like the idea of the proposal. My biggest concern, as someone else mentioned, is the applicant’s track record. They seem relatively new to the community and I can’t see much GitHub history, so I don’t have enough confidence yet. I hope this individual continues to engage with the ecosystem.

  • Hanh: For this particular proposal, I can say they have done some work. I’ve seen them working on the spec and interacting with other teams to come up with a standard, so there’s a real person behind it. But again, I can’t vouch for whether it would meet the requirement, because there’s no ZIP.

  • Paul: OK, that’s helpful. Perhaps getting a ZIP would change my view, so thank you.

  • Zerodartz: I also think a final ZIP would make this proposal much stronger. In current form I wouldn’t approve it. Gguy: We’ll leave this open and go back to the applicant to ask for a ZIP as a deliverable.

  • Remains open

  • Zocial World — Privacy-First Social, Learning and Collaboration Platform for Zcash

  • Applicant requests $45,000 over about 4 months to harden and expand Zocial World, an open-source 3D social world in the browser for the Zcash community, with a public beta already running. Funding covers beta hardening and Watch Hall events, then a Learning Valley and “Testnet Academy” with an AI learning guide, then project discovery and contributor pathways, then a security review, original 3D art, accessibility work and a production-readiness push. The team is three people: two full-stack developers and one 3D artist.

  • Artkor: I think we’ve already seen that people aren’t particularly interested in 3D virtual worlds as platforms for social interaction. If you ever see me vote to approve something like this, you can be sure I’ve been taken hostage by North Korean hackers. I decline.

  • Hanh: It’s a pretty generic game, more like the 3D avatar platforms that were popular in the Facebook days. These can be generated very quickly and don’t provide much value. I decline as well.

  • Zerodartz: I agree this doesn’t have much value. Something like this was more popular maybe five years ago, but I haven’t seen anything like it recently that is crypto-related and popular. I’m going to decline.

  • Paul: I’ll decline as well.

  • Gguy: I agree. There’s a little bit of fun to this project, but history often shows it’s hard to get meaningful engagement on these platforms. That would have to be proven first. Decline.

  • Declined

  • Zecboat: Wake v1, a custom Halo 2 circuit for note lineage

  • Applicant requests $61,400 over about 7 months to take Wake-v1 through independent review and release. Wake-v1 is a custom Halo 2 zero-knowledge circuit that lets a recipient check on-chain that a layer-two shielded asset (Applicant’s “ZMAP” format, used here for NFT-style collections) descends from the issuer’s original note. The check doesn’t require viewing keys for earlier transfers. Funding also covers Zecboat, Applicant’s Debian desktop wallet (versions 0.8 through 1.0), 12 tutorial videos, 3 workshops, 9 commissioned art collections, 9 blog posts and a 3-part research report.

  • Artkor: I’d be willing to support this experiment, but only if we can be confident the proposed solution is truly decentralized and resilient against attacks. At this point I’m not convinced it provides both guarantees, so I decline.

  • Hanh: The proposal uses “ZSA on L2” as a pitch line, but that’s not really what it is, and it doesn’t give you the guarantees ZSAs offer. It places a zero-knowledge proof in an Orchard note memo to prove that the note you see descends from the genesis of that particular item. It’s similar to the colored coin approach, with a zero-knowledge proof instead of visibility into the transaction tree. There are a lot of limitations: you have to use their wallet, and if you make a mistake or use a regular wallet at any point, the asset is burned and can never be recovered. What you get is a proof of lineage, not a proof of ownership, so if you want to trade it you can’t prove you hold it. These limitations are in their white paper, so they aren’t being dishonest, but they’re never mentioned on the website, and I’m not comfortable with that marketing. I don’t really like it, but we won’t see many projects like this, so I’m on the fence.

  • Gguy: I’m leaning a bit more positively on this today. It took me a long time to get my head around it, and the website doesn’t help. The site feels like it was generated as a proof-of-concept site rather than a full and accurate explanation of the technical details, so it would be good if the applicant could clear that up. Otherwise, I think this is the type of missing technology that is good for us to explore. Whether or not it leads directly to a product used by many users, I think it’s worth the exploration. I’m ready to approve today.

  • Hanh: I would not approve if they keep “ZSA” on their website. It’s not a ZSA, and I think they are riding the coattails of work other people have done.

  • Gguy: That’s fair, I’d agree. I’d like to see that cleared up.

  • Paul: I’m curious about the proposal, but it’s not written in a way that’s compelling to me, so perhaps I’m missing something. If this is about ZSA-type functionality, or additional assets on top of Zcash, I’m not sure I’m interested unless I see strong community support. If it can be rewritten to be more understandable to the community, with community support behind it, I might change my mind. At this time, I would not approve.

  • Zerodartz: In the long term I’m open to ZSAs or similar things, but in the short term I don’t see this being that useful. We’ve seen some experiments with ZSA-type assets in recent months, and while they’re interesting, there have been a lot of shady projects popping up, and it’s hard for new users to understand what they are actually getting. I’m declining.

  • Gguy: OK, that’s a decline today, four to one. If the applicant wishes to keep exploring this, I’d encourage them to clear up their site and how they present and describe their work. Some of the statements imply delivering something similar to ZSAs. You could argue there are similarities, since it’s shielded and an asset, but it can be misleading.

  • Hanh: It’s not a ZSA because there’s no value and it’s not splittable. It’s much more similar to an NFT. I would accept something like a Zcash NFT, but definitely not a ZSA.

  • Gguy: I hope they explore that more, and I’d encourage the applicant to come back with a clearer proposal. But keep in mind I’m only one of five.

  • Declined (Gguy approved)

  • Zcash BuildPath India: Four-City Developer Onboarding Pilot

  • Applicant requests $17,600 over 14 weeks for “Zcash BuildPath India,” a developer onboarding pilot in four cities: Bhopal, Indore, Delhi and Noida. Each city gets a four-hour workshop and a ten-hour build day, followed by shared clinics and a 30-day revision follow-up. The targets are 160 unique builders, at least 12 qualifying MIT-licensed prototypes, at least 6 with a reproducible testnet payment flow, and a reusable teaching kit. The work builds on Veil, Applicant’s AI-assisted Zcash diagnostic prototype.

  • Artkor: Of the next three event proposals, I’d only support the third one, the Bolivian university initiative, because the budget is small enough that I’m comfortable approving it without hesitation. I’m not convinced the other two justify much larger budgets at this stage, especially since these applicants have never represented our community before. I wouldn’t feel comfortable committing that much funding without knowing what to expect from them. I decline this one.

  • Paul: In general I have some reservations about funding developer-focused initiatives at this time. If this were more university-oriented, that might change my view, but developers have ample tools to get started quickly without these workshops. I’m much more interested in driving adoption with regular users, awareness and other community efforts. I decline.

  • Gguy: I’m also a reject.

  • Zerodartz: It’s a reject from me, since this is a new team to Zcash and it’s not a super small ask. We also have a team in India already doing some events and participating at hackathons.

  • Declined

  • Zcash Early Builders Lab (ZEBL) Cape Town

  • Applicant requests $47,300 over about 3 months to run a 2-day workshop and mini-hackathon in Cape Town for 80+ students aged 16–22, followed by a 30-day “Young Builders Circle.” Students would learn zero-knowledge cryptography and financial privacy, with hands-on testnet-only exercises (a “Shielded Arcade” wallet game) and coding tracks in Kotlin/Swift, TypeScript and Rust. There’s also a parent/educator session and an open-source curriculum. The plan names an 8-person team.

  • Hanh: For me it’s the same reasons as the previous one.

  • Zerodartz: It’s quite a similar idea to the India developer grant, a bit bigger, but still a decline for me, since the team doesn’t have any track record with Zcash yet as far as I can see..

  • Paul: Decline here as well.

  • Gguy: Declined.

  • Declined

  • CENTIREINGS Zcash Market Segmentation & Comparative Intelligence

  • Applicant requests $22,500 over 3 months to extend its existing quantitative benchmark of 20 cryptoassets (“EXP300-B”) into a Zcash-specific study. The study would reproduce ZEC’s historical market-behavior profile, place ZEC within the 20-asset universe under the same rules, and test whether that classification holds up on newer data. The output is a public “ZEC Market Segmentation Map” with a report, methodology and reproducibility materials.

  • Paul: I would reject this. Marketing and ecosystem research are better placed within the projects that are onboarding people. They have every incentive to do this kind of work, and I don’t think ZCG needs to do it for the ecosystem broadly.

  • Gguy: I’ll be declining as well.

  • Zerodartz: It’s quite expensive for a research grant. We have a lot of people doing all sorts of things with data and can also do something similar, if there is demand for this sort of info. I’m declining.

  • Artkor: Declined.

  • Declined

  • Zcash Privacy & Adoption in Two Bolivian Universities by BlockivIA

  • Applicant requests $1,500 over about 5 weeks to run three Zcash privacy and adoption workshops for at least 100 university students in Bolivia: two in person at UMSA in La Paz and one virtual with UAGRM in Santa Cruz. Each workshop covers financial privacy and Zcash basics, wallet onboarding and hands-on transactions with real ZEC, funded from a fixed $400 pool. The workshops are documented with attendance, feedback, interviews and a summary video.

  • Artkor: I approve this one.

  • Zerodartz: While I’d usually say to take this to ZecHub, the ask is low and I noticed ZecHub is running low on its yearly budget for this kind of community project. So I’m ready to approve this one and see what this experiment results in.

  • Gguy: I agree. This is a reasonable ask, and we’ve seen through past events that there may be value in this. I’m willing to give it a go. Approved.

  • Paul: I approve.

  • Hanh: I approve as well. I saw pictures, his website and his documentation, so there’s prior work, and unlike the other proposals it doesn’t seem to be AI-generated. Even if he delivers a fraction of what he offers, given what he’s asking for, that’s reasonable.

  • Approved

  • Zcash RPC Streaming Redaction Audit

  • Applicant requests $6,000 over 8 weeks (starting March 1, 2027) for an independent study of whether sensitive values, such as keys or seeds, can slip past log redaction when Zcash RPC-style messages are logged in chunks. It would compare exact streaming redaction against buffer-then-redact approaches on a synthetic corpus of 200 messages and release the test harness under MIT.

  • Artkor: I’m not sure about this one. I agree with Hanh. Decline.

  • Hanh: I don’t see the case for this. The core premise is that redacting sensitive literals from complete messages may miss them when a literal is split across chunks. Why build a whole project around that? You can check that it isn’t the case. There’s no justification for the premise, and it seems very far-fetched. I reject.

  • Zerodartz: It’s a decline from me. This grant seems confusing to me.

  • Paul: Decline.

  • Gguy: I struggled to get my head around this one. If I’m missing something, I’m happy for the applicant to let me know. Otherwise, reject.

  • Declined

  • Zcash 中文入门包 / Zcash Chinese Onboarding Pack

  • Applicant requests $5,000 over about 3 months to produce a Simplified Chinese onboarding pack. It covers about 20 core ZecHub pages translated into zh-CN and submitted as PRs to ZecHub, a shielded-wallet tutorial with screenshots, a glossary of about 150 terms from English to Chinese, and three long-form articles for Zhihu, WeChat or Mirror.

  • Hanh: I think the Chinese market is important, and having pages in Chinese is very important too. ZecHub currently has several languages, but they’re all AI-translated, so I don’t know the quality of those pages. I’d like to support this; $5K isn’t asking too much. I also don’t want the applicant to just use AI translation, and I’m not sure how we’d verify that.

  • Artkor: I agree with Hanh, and I would approve this grant.

  • Paul: I wouldn’t approve it at this time. If I understand correctly, the applicant plans to work with ZecHub. I’d like to see ZecHub recommend to us that this is useful to them, and then I’d have a different view.

  • Hanh: We could involve them and ask. I think they have a DAO, so this could potentially go through their DAO first.

  • Paul: I think that would be ideal.

  • Gguy: I also see discussions about adjusting this grant as of 13 hours ago, so I’m happy to keep exploring what they come up with. We’ll leave this one open and continue discussions.

  • Remains open

  • zreceipt: payment disclosures for shielded Zcash (ZIP 311)

  • Applicant requests $40,000 over about 6 months to turn zreceipt into a full ZIP 311 implementation. zreceipt is a working tool, already live on mainnet, that lets a Zcash user prove one shielded payment (amount, recipient and memo) through a shareable link without revealing their balance or other transactions, with support for Sapling, Orchard and Ironwood. The grant would fund a Rust/WebAssembly SDK published on crates.io and npm, verification through lightwalletd or offline, the “spend-authority” half of ZIP 311 (proving the presenter actually sent the payment), a “Share receipt” feature contributed to an open-source wallet, and a pilot with a bank, a licensed crypto exchange and a law firm in Kyrgyzstan.

  • Artkor: I looked into the applicant’s background but couldn’t find a convincing track record in software development in general. Apparently the Rust developer who would implement the core functionality hasn’t even been hired yet. As I understand it, ZIP 311 already describes how to prove a specific shielded payment without revealing other transactions, but it still lacks a complete working implementation. Once one is available, I don’t see major obstacles to integrating it into existing wallets and payment systems like BTCPay Server or CipherPay, so I’m not convinced we need a separate product. I’d really like to see ZIP 311 move forward, but I’m not sure approving this particular proposal would help achieve that.

  • Hanh: I think the applicant needs more engagement from the community for something as important as payment disclosure. There have been a lot of discussions around this going back to Sprout. The fact that it isn’t in the protocol yet means either it’s very hard, which I don’t see why it would be, or there isn’t enough interest to formalize it. They’ve put some work into designing something, but it’s not clear it would be adopted, and too many ZIPs in this area have been abandoned. I decline because there’s no ZIP commitment.

  • Paul: I also decline.

  • Gguy: When you say ZIP commitment, do you mean going through the actual ZIP process rather than just posting a draft? They mention updating ZIP 311 with Orchard/Ironwood spend-authority text and test vectors in milestone 3.

  • Hanh: ZIP 311 is still in draft. That’s what I mean by abandoned: it’s very old and has never progressed beyond draft.

  • Gguy: So your concern is that even if they update the ZIP, no progress will be made. I’d like to see work continue on receipts; I think it’s something Zcash needs at some point. I’m unsure how this works with the Tachyon-era protocol, but I encourage the exploration. I’m not ready to vote on this one today.

  • Paul: I’m willing to leave it open until next time to see if there’s any further engagement.

  • Hanh: If the applicant wants to move this in the right direction, he needs to contact str4d and discuss what would make the ZIP go forward. ZIP 311 is from six years ago and is still in draft.

  • Gguy: I might reach out as well to see if there’s interest among the existing developer groups in helping progress this.

  • Remains open
